title: Ruth as a type of the Gentiles and the legal problem of her entry
english: And the name of the second was Ruth (Ruth 1:4). Ruth bears a type of the Gentiles, for she left behind her ancestral customs and was joined to the Israelite way of life. But we must ask how Ruth, being a Moabite, entered the assembly of God when the law forbids a Moabite from entering (Deuteronomy 23:3). And seeking this, I apply the saying: “The law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the lawless and disobedient” (1 Timothy 1:9).

added_allusions.reason: The opening lemma quotes the verse under comment: the Greek Καὶ ὄνομα τῇ δευτέρᾳ Ῥούθ closely echoes Ruth 1:4 in the Septuagint (καὶ ὄνομα τῇ γυναικὶ τῇ δευτέρᾳ Ρουθ), the naming of the second daughter-in-law, on which the whole scrap comments.

Origen states the bar in the law's own collocation: the Greek μὴ εἰσελθεῖν Μοαβίτην εἰς Ἐκκλησίαν Θεοῦ (a Moabite, to enter, the assembly of God) reproduces Deuteronomy 23:3 (Septuagint: οὐκ εἰσελεύσεται Ἀμμανίτης καὶ Μωαβίτης εἰς ἐκκλησίαν κυρίου). Origen cites it simply as the law; Nehemiah 13:1 is a later restatement of the same bar and is not entered separately.

Recorded in all eight justification files for this work (methods quotation and wording) and already applied inline in the published English; the enrichment adds this entry only. The Greek quote Δικαίῳ δὲ νόμος οὐ κεῖται, ἀλλὰ ἀδίκοις καὶ ἀνυποτάκτοις is near-verbatim 1 Timothy 1:9 with one variant: Origen's form reads ἀδίκοις (for the unjust) where the New Testament text reads ἀνόμοις (for the lawless), so the quote is not exact at that word.

orientation: Origen opens his commentary on Ruth by identifying Ruth as a type of the Gentiles and then raises the legal difficulty that the law forbids a Moabite from entering the assembly of God.
